title: Screen time, problematic screen use, and eating disorder symptoms among early adolescents: findings from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study
authors: Chu J, Ganson KT, Testa A, Al-shoaibi AAA, Jackson DB, Rodgers RF, He J, Baker FC, Nagata JM
journal: Eating and Weight Disorders - Studies on Anorexia, Bulimia and Obesity (2024) 29:57

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted logistic regression of year-2 eating disorder symptoms on baseline social media hours/day, adjusted for baseline parent-reported ED symptom, BMI percentile, anxiety and BAS reward responsiveness
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, right-hand 'Social media use' columns (p. 6); results text p. 4; interpreted in Discussion pp. 6-7
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal. Social media use is measured at the ABCD baseline visit (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the five eating disorder symptoms are measured once, by youth-report KSADS-5, at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020). Each symptom is a single binary follow-up outcome (no repeated measures, no time interaction). Because youth were not asked the ED items at baseline, the parent-reported baseline KSADS-5 version of the same symptom is entered as a covariate. Social media and total screen time are reported in separate columns of Table 2; the paper does not state that social media models adjust for other screen modalities.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 4.0, 21 U.S. sites. Analytic N = 10,246 after excluding participants missing screen time or eating disorder symptom data (N = 1,552, 13.1%; included vs excluded comparison in Additional file 1 Table S1, not bundled in the PDF). Missing baseline sociodemographic data were filled by Gaussian normal regression imputation in Stata. Baseline (Table 1, weighted): mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.6% female, 51.4% male; 54.4% White, 19.7% Latino/Hispanic, 16.0% Black, 5.4% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.4% Other; 45.0% household income < $75,000; 81.2% parent with college education or more. The N per Table 2 cell is not printed separately.
primary_models.iv: Baseline social media use in hours per day from the self-reported ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (social media item, e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter), asked separately for typical weekday and weekend day and combined as ((weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)) / 7. Entered as a continuous variable; ORs are per additional hour/day. Table 1: social media 0.1 (SD 0.4) hours. (Total screen time, the headline exposure, is a six-modality sum including TV, videos and video games and is excluded below.)
primary_models.dv: Five binary youth-reported KSADS-5 eating disorder symptoms at year two, each modeled separately: fear of obesity (worried all the time about weight or becoming fat for a month or longer), self-worth tied to weight, inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (yes to any of eating only minimal-calorie foods, exercising a lot, vomiting, water pills/laxatives/diet pills), binge eating, and distress with binge eating. Year-two prevalence (Table 1): 1.4%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 7.5%, 2.9% respectively.

primary_models.equation: logit P(ED_symptom_Y2[i] = 1) = b0 + b1*SM_hours_baseline[i] + b2..b6*race/ethnicity + b7*sex + b8*income + b9*parent_ed + site fixed effects + b10*parent_ED_symptom_baseline[i] + b11*BMI_percentile + b12*anxiety_tscore + b13*BAS_reward; OR = exp(b1) per 1 hour/day
primary_models.estimation: Multiple logistic regression in Stata 18.0 using svyset/svy commands with ABCD propensity weights (American Community Survey raking to age, sex and race/ethnicity). Site entered as a covariate; no random effects or family clustering described. Significance at p < 0.05 (bold in table); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Interactions between sex and the exposures were tested, were not significant, and results were not stratified by sex (no numbers printed). Age is named as a confounder in the Methods text but is not listed in the Table 2 covariate footnote. No unadjusted model is printed. No sensitivity analyses reported.

primary_models.name: Survey-weighted logistic regression of year-2 eating disorder symptoms on concurrent problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic mobile phone use (MPIQ), adjusted for BMI percentile, anxiety and BAS reward responsiveness
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 3 (p. 6); results text pp. 4-5; interpreted in Discussion pp. 6-7
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. SMAQ and MPIQ were first administered at the year-two follow-up (2018-2020), the same visit at which the youth-reported KSADS-5 eating disorder symptoms were measured. Each problematic-use scale and each symptom is modeled separately (2 IVs x 5 DVs). Baseline covariates are included, but unlike M1 the baseline parent-reported ED symptom is not in the Table 3 covariate list. Authors note they could not test prospective associations because problematic use was not measured at baseline.
primary_models.sample: Subsamples of the N = 10,246 ABCD Release 4.0 analytic cohort: SMAQ models n = 5,587 (only youth reporting at least one social media account were asked the SMAQ); MPIQ models n = 7,280 (only youth reporting having a mobile phone were asked the MPIQ). Demographics are reported only for the full 10,246 (Table 1; see M1), not for these subsamples.
primary_models.iv: (a) Problematic social media use: 6-item adolescent Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ), modeled after the Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, items rated 1 (never) to 6 (very often); Table 1 score 1.9 (SD 0.9). (b) Problematic mobile phone use: 8-item Mobile Phone Involvement Questionnaire (MPIQ), items rated 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree); Table 1 score 3.1 (SD 1.1). The magnitudes in Table 1 suggest item-mean scoring, but the paper does not state the scoring or the unit of the OR (presumably per 1-point increase in the scale score). Entered continuously.
primary_models.dv: Same five binary year-two KSADS-5 youth-reported symptoms as M1 (fear of obesity, self-worth tied to weight, inappropriate compensatory behaviors, binge eating, distress with binge eating). Prevalence within the SMAQ and MPIQ subsamples is not reported; full-sample prevalence is 1.4%, 1.6%, 0.7%, 7.5%, 2.9%.

primary_models.equation: logit P(ED_symptom_Y2[i] = 1) = b0 + b1*ProblematicUse_Y2[i] + b2..b6*race/ethnicity + b7*sex + b8*income + b9*parent_ed + site fixed effects + b10*BMI_percentile_baseline + b11*anxiety_tscore_baseline + b12*BAS_reward_baseline; ProblematicUse = SMAQ or MPIQ score; OR = exp(b1)
primary_models.estimation: Same as M1: Stata 18.0 svy logistic regression with ABCD ACS-based propensity weights; site as covariate; no random effects; alpha 0.05 with no multiple-comparison correction; sex interactions tested and non-significant (not printed). Age named as a confounder in Methods text but absent from the Table 3 covariate footnote. SMAQ and MPIQ are entered in separate models (no mutual adjustment reported).

excluded_models.model: Baseline total screen time -> year-2 eating disorder symptoms (logistic, same spec as M1)
excluded_models.why: Total screen time is the sum of six modalities including television/movies, online videos and video games; it bundles non-phone/non-SM activities. The social media component is broken out separately and extracted as M1; texting and video chat are not separately modeled. Fails FT-IC2 Step 2.
Reported only as not statistically significant; no interaction coefficients or sex-stratified estimates printed.

excluded_models.model: Included vs excluded participant comparison and KSADS-5 item details
excluded_models.location: Additional file 1, Tables S1 and S2 (online supplement, not in PDF)
excluded_models.why: Descriptive/measurement material with no phone/SM-outcome estimate; supplement not bundled in the PDF.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: per 1 additional hour/day of baseline social media use. M2: per 1-unit increase in SMAQ or MPIQ score (unit not explicitly stated; item-mean scale assumed from Table 1 means).
d_transformation.notes: Both models report adjusted ORs with 95% CIs, so the Chinn conversion applies directly and p0 is not needed. p0 values given in dv_axis are the full-sample (N = 10,246, weighted) year-two prevalences from Table 1 (p. 5); prevalences within the SMAQ (n = 5,587) and MPIQ (n = 7,280) subsamples are not reported. SD_IV values from Table 1 (p. 5): social media 0.4 hours/day (baseline), SMAQ 0.9, MPIQ 1.1; these are full-sample/subsample descriptives as printed and could be used to rescale ORs to a per-SD contrast (ln OR x SD_IV) if a per-SD comparison is wanted. Because social media hours have a very small SD (0.4 h), the per-hour OR of 1.55 corresponds to a much smaller per-SD effect; per-hour d values are not directly comparable to per-SD d values from other papers.

extraction_flags: (1) The paper never states the scoring unit for SMAQ and MPIQ, so for M2 the contrast is assumed to be per 1 point on an item-mean score. That assumption comes from the Table 1 means (1.9 and 3.1) and the item ranges. (2) The Methods text names age as a confounder, but neither the Table 2 nor the Table 3 covariate footnote lists it. The extraction follows the footnotes and flags the gap. Smaller points: the p0 values are full-sample year-two prevalences from Table 1. Prevalences within the SMAQ (n=5,587) and MPIQ (n=7,280) subsamples are not reported, but Chinn's OR-to-d conversion does not need p0. Table 1 does not say outright that the 'Social media (hours)' SD of 0.4 is from baseline; it is read as baseline because it sits under the table's 'baseline' header. Per-cell N is not printed for Table 2. The Table 3 models leave out the baseline parent-reported eating disorder symptom covariate, so their specification differs from M1. The total-screen-time column is excluded as a mixed composite. The supplement (Tables S1 and S2) is not in the PDF. I checked all 15 ORs, CIs and p-values against the table text pulled from the PDF.
